explanations.answer: Get circumcised by the custom of Moses
explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The men from Judea tell the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” (Acts 15:1) One sentence, and look at the council it sets off. I've seen small things stir up a big mess, but that one is the champion.

explanations.answer: Offer a sacrifice in the temple
explanations.explanation: Good thinking, but these men never mention a sacrifice. They say, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” (Acts 15:1) The thing they name is circumcision. That's the claim Paul and Barnabas push back on.

Feasts in Jerusalem don't come up in what these men say, friend. They teach the brothers, “Unless you are circumcised according to the custom of Moses, you cannot be saved.” (Acts 15:1) Keeping every feast would be a whole calendar of batches, but they name only one requirement. That one requirement is circumcision.

Jerusalem it is. Paul, Barnabas and some other believers are appointed to go up there to see the apostles and elders about this question (Acts 15:2). They aren't going alone, either. They're sent as a group. When a question gets this big, it helps to bring it to the leaders instead of arguing in the hallway all week.

Damascus is a real city, but it's not the one named here. The text says Paul, Barnabas and some other believers were appointed to go up to Jerusalem (Acts 15:2). That's where the apostles and elders are. So pack the bags for Jerusalem, friend.

Tarsus doesn't show up in this part of the story, friend. Paul and Barnabas are appointed, along with some other believers, to go up to Jerusalem to see the apostles and elders about this question (Acts 15:2). That's the destination. The apostles and elders are the ones they're going to see.

Joy, and a lot of it. As Paul and Barnabas pass through Phoenicia and Samaria, they recount the conversion of the Gentiles, “bringing great joy to all the brothers.” (Acts 15:3) Good news travels fast when people are glad to hear it. I think those brothers were smiling long after the visitors left.

Not at all, friend. The text says the news brought “great joy to all the brothers.” (Acts 15:3) The trouble comes from the men who showed up in Antioch teaching something else. Along this road, the news about the Gentiles lands as good news.

explanations.answer: They ask to see some proof
explanations.explanation: No proof is requested in this verse. Paul and Barnabas recount the conversion of the Gentiles, and it brings “great joy to all the brothers.” (Acts 15:3) The brothers hear the news and they're glad. That's the whole reaction the text gives.

True. The text says some believers “from the party of the Pharisees stood up and declared, ‘The Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses.’” (Acts 15:5) They name it right out loud, in front of everybody. Now the council has a real question on its table.

It's true, friend. The text says the ones who stood up were believers “from the party of the Pharisees.” (Acts 15:5) They declared that the Gentiles must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses. It's right there in the verse.

Believe is the word. Peter, one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Luke 6:13-14), says God made a choice that the Gentiles would hear the message of the gospel from his lips “and believe.” (Acts 15:7) He's reminding the room of something God already did. It's hard to argue with what God already did.

Obey sounds close, but Peter says something else. He says God chose that the Gentiles would hear the message of the gospel from his lips “and believe.” (Acts 15:7) Peter is one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Luke 6:13-14), and he's telling the room what he saw himself. Hearing, then believing.

Rejoicing does show up later in this chapter, but not in Peter's sentence. He says God chose that the Gentiles would hear the gospel from his lips “and believe.” (Acts 15:7) Peter is one of Jesus' twelve apostles (Luke 6:13-14). The word he lands on is believe.

explanations.answer: By giving them the Holy Spirit
explanations.explanation: Right on target. Peter says God, who knows the heart, showed His approval “by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us.” (Acts 15:8) Notice the words just as He did to us. God gave the same gift to both groups. I wouldn't argue with that kind of proof.

explanations.answer: By sending them a new prophet
explanations.explanation: A new prophet isn't mentioned in Peter's speech. He says God, who knows the heart, showed His approval “by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us.” (Acts 15:8) The sign was the Holy Spirit. And it was the very same gift the Jewish believers got.

explanations.answer: By healing all of their sick
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't talk about healing here, friend. He says God showed His approval “by giving the Holy Spirit to them, just as He did to us.” (Acts 15:8) That's the sign he points to. God gave the Gentiles the same Spirit He gave to Peter and the others.

Faith, friend. Peter says God “made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith.” (Acts 15:9) No distinction means no first-class line and second-class line. Same God, same cleansing, same way in.

Sacrifice isn't the word Peter uses. He says God “made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith.” (Acts 15:9) The cleansing came by faith. That's the answer Peter gives the whole room.

That's a tempting one, since the law is the topic of the whole meeting. But Peter says God “made no distinction between us and them, for He cleansed their hearts by faith.” (Acts 15:9) The cleansing is by faith. Peter doesn't say by law.

It's the opposite, friend. Peter calls it “a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear.” (Acts 15:10) That means they haven't been able to bear it. He's talking about the Jewish believers and their fathers, and he includes himself.

False is right. Peter calls it “a yoke that neither we nor our fathers have been able to bear.” (Acts 15:10) He says it about himself and the other Jewish believers, and about their fathers too. He's pointing out that nobody in the room carried it.

explanations.answer: Through the grace of the Lord Jesus
explanations.explanation: That's it. Peter says, “we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.” (Acts 15:11) Just as they are. Jewish believers and Gentiles, saved the same way. Peter wraps up his whole speech in one sentence.

explanations.answer: Through keeping the law of Moses
explanations.explanation: That's what the Pharisee party was pushing, but it's not Peter's answer. He says, “we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.” (Acts 15:11) Saved through grace, and the same for both groups. That's his last word on it.

explanations.answer: Through being the sons of Abraham
explanations.explanation: Peter doesn't mention Abraham in this speech. He says, “we believe it is through the grace of the Lord Jesus that we are saved, just as they are.” (Acts 15:11) The way of being saved is the grace of the Lord Jesus. It's the same way for the Jewish believers and the Gentiles.

explanations.answer: Signs and wonders God did among the Gentiles
explanations.explanation: Yes. The whole assembly fell silent as they listened to Barnabas and Paul “describing the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.” (Acts 15:12) Notice who gets the credit in that sentence. God did them, through Barnabas and Paul. Those two didn't take the credit, and I like that.

explanations.answer: Their plans to go and preach in Rome
explanations.explanation: Rome doesn't come up here, friend. The assembly listens as Barnabas and Paul describe “the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.” (Acts 15:12) They're telling what already happened. Nobody in the room is hearing travel plans.

explanations.answer: The new rules of the church in Antioch
explanations.explanation: No new rules from Antioch are mentioned in this verse. The assembly falls silent as Barnabas and Paul describe “the signs and wonders God had done among the Gentiles through them.” (Acts 15:12) They're giving a report of what God did. The room is quiet and listening.

That's right. James, the one who speaks after Barnabas and Paul finish, says, “The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written.” (Acts 15:15) He doesn't only lean on what Peter saw. He brings what was written down long before. Now there's testimony and Scripture on the same page.

The Pharisee party spoke up earlier, but James doesn't bring them in here. He says, “The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written.” (Acts 15:15) That's what lines up with what Peter said. James is the one speaking, and he points to the prophets.

The teaching from Judea is what started the whole argument, so it's not what James lines up with Peter. James says, “The words of the prophets agree with this, as it is written.” (Acts 15:15) It's the prophets he points to. He's the one speaking, right after Barnabas and Paul.

explanations.answer: The remnant of men and all the Gentiles
explanations.explanation: You've got it. The quote says, “…so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name…” (Acts 15:17) The Gentiles are right there in the words of the prophet. James picked a good verse for the room.

The word only doesn't fit here, friend. The quote says, “…so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name…” (Acts 15:17) The Gentiles are named in the words themselves. Nobody gets left out of that sentence.

David's fallen tent is what gets rebuilt, but the quote doesn't stop with David's house. It says, “…so that the remnant of men may seek the Lord, and all the Gentiles who are called by My name…” (Acts 15:17) The Gentiles are named right in the words. That's why James brought them up.

It's the other way around, friend. James says, “…we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God.” (Acts 15:19) He isn't asking them to take on the whole law. He's saying don't make it hard for them.

False is right. James says, “…we should not cause trouble for the Gentiles who are turning to God.” (Acts 15:19) He doesn't ask for the whole law of Moses. He says not to cause trouble for the ones turning to God, and that settles the question.

That's the one. James says to abstain “from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.” (Acts 15:20) Four things, and sexual immorality is one of them. Short list, friend, and all four are right there in the verse.

The Sabbath does come up in the next verse, but not on this list. James says to abstain “from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.” (Acts 15:20) Those are the four things. Breaking the Sabbath isn't one of them.

Interest isn't on James's list. He says to abstain “from food polluted by idols, from sexual immorality, from the meat of strangled animals, and from blood.” (Acts 15:20) That's four things in total. Sexual immorality is the one that matches this card.

Silas it is. The text says they chose “Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers.” (Acts 15:22) They send leaders, not just messengers. The whole church is behind this decision, and these two carry it to Antioch.

Timothy isn't named in this passage. The text says they chose “Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers.” (Acts 15:22) Silas is the one who goes with Judas. The two of them travel to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas.

Titus doesn't appear in this story, friend. The text says they chose “Judas called Barsabbas and Silas, two leaders among the brothers.” (Acts 15:22) Silas is the second name. He and Judas head to Antioch with Paul and Barnabas.

The letter says the opposite. It says, “…some went out from us without our authorization and unsettled you, troubling your minds by what they said.” (Acts 15:24) Without our authorization. The leaders are making it plain that those men didn't speak for them.

False is right. The letter says, “…some went out from us without our authorization and unsettled you, troubling your minds by what they said.” (Acts 15:24) The leaders didn't authorize those men. They say so right at the start, so nobody is confused about who said what.

explanations.answer: To tell them in person what the letter says
explanations.explanation: Yes. The letter says, “Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas to tell you in person the same things we are writing.” (Acts 15:27) So the message comes two ways, on paper and by voice. That's some good backup, friend. Nobody is left guessing what the leaders meant.

explanations.answer: To collect an offering for the church in Jerusalem
explanations.explanation: No offering is mentioned in the letter. It says, “Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas to tell you in person the same things we are writing.” (Acts 15:27) They're coming to say the same thing the letter says. It's a message, not a collection.

explanations.answer: To appoint new elders for the church in Antioch
explanations.explanation: Appointing elders isn't what the letter says. It says, “Therefore we are sending Judas and Silas to tell you in person the same things we are writing.” (Acts 15:27) Their job is to say it in person. The same words, spoken out loud.

That's right. The letter says, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements.” (Acts 15:28) The Holy Spirit is named first in that sentence. This decision wasn't just a vote at a meeting. It's the Spirit and the leaders together.

A high priest isn't named in the letter, friend. It says, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements.” (Acts 15:28) The Holy Spirit comes first in the sentence. The apostles and elders are the others.

The Pharisee party spoke earlier in the meeting, but the letter doesn't name them. It says, “It seemed good to the Holy Spirit and to us not to burden you with anything beyond these essential requirements.” (Acts 15:28) The Holy Spirit is who gets named. The apostles and elders stand right beside Him in that sentence.

True. The text says, “When the people read it, they rejoiced at its encouraging message.” (Acts 15:31) After the sharp debate and the long road, that's a happy ending for the letter. Real encouragement is a gift, friend. They got it in writing.
It's true, friend. The text says, “When the people read it, they rejoiced at its encouraging message.” (Acts 15:31) They didn't groan or argue. They rejoiced.

Prophets is right. The text says Judas and Silas, “who themselves were prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers.” (Acts 15:32) They didn't only hand over the letter. They stayed and talked, and the brothers were encouraged and strengthened. Messengers who bring the news and then bring some heart with it are a gift.

Priests isn't the word the text uses. It says Judas and Silas, “who themselves were prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers.” (Acts 15:32) The word is prophets. They had plenty to say to the brothers in Antioch.

Levites aren't mentioned in this passage, friend. The text says Judas and Silas, “who themselves were prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers.” (Acts 15:32) They're called prophets. And they used their words to build the brothers up.
